subject: 인더스 문명의 도시 계획
title: A civilization that built by the grid
content: The cities of the ancient Indus civilization were laid out with a care that still surprises the archaeologists who excavate them. Streets met at right angles, residential blocks followed a common measure, and the bricks used across a very wide region shared identical proportions. This is unusual, because most early towns grew by addition rather than by design, and their lanes bend wherever an older wall once stood. What the archaeology reveals here is a different origin entirely. The drainage alone would mark this civilization as remarkable. Covered channels ran beneath the main streets, houses discharged waste into them through clay pipes, and settling basins caught solids before the flow continued. Such a system demands more than technical skill, since it demands agreement about where the lines will run and who will keep them clear. Therefore the plan implies authority of some kind, although its form remains obscure. That obscurity is the central puzzle of this era. No royal tombs have been identified, no palace rises above the rest, and the surviving images show no ruler enthroned in majesty. Other ancient civilizations left us kings carved in stone; this one did not. Some scholars read the absence as evidence that power rested with councils or with priests, while others suspect that the insignia of rank were made of cloth and timber and have simply decayed. The script might settle the question, but nobody can read it. The signs appear on small seals, the inscriptions are extremely brief, and no lengthy bilingual text has emerged to break the code. Consequently we understand the layout of the streets far better than the names of those who walked them. What the site finally offers is a plan without a narrative. We can trace the water, the walls, and the granaries, yet the century by century record that other ancient civilizations supply is missing here.

subject: 히타이트 제국의 철
title: The empire that worked the harder metal
content: Through a long stretch of the ancient world, bronze was the metal that mattered. It cast cleanly, it held an edge, and the exchange of tin and copper bound distant courts together. Iron was known, yet it remained rare, since the ore had to be worked at heat for a long period and the result was often inferior to good bronze. The transition came slowly, and one empire has long been credited with beginning it. The Hittites held the high plateau of Anatolia for several centuries, and the archives from their capital mention iron in ways that suggest control. One letter, sent to a foreign king, apologises that no iron can be supplied at present and offers a single blade instead. Historians once read that note as evidence of a guarded craft held closely by the crown. More recent scholarship has softened the reading. Iron objects appear in the ancient region well before this empire rose, and they appear beyond its reach as well, therefore no single court can have monopolised the technique. What the letter records is scarcity rather than secrecy, and scarcity suits a metal that demanded enormous labour to produce in useful quantities. The wider adoption of iron seems to follow the collapse of the old order rather than its height. When the bronze networks failed near the close of that era, the long routes carrying tin were severed, and smiths turned to an ore lying close at hand almost everywhere. Iron prevailed because it was local, not because it was superior. This is a valuable lesson about how such transitions occur within any civilization. A new material rarely wins on merit alone. It waits for the older system to fail, and then it spreads rapidly, because the ore lies beneath the feet of every village rather than at the far end of a road.

subject: 페니키아 항해와 지중해 식민
title: Traders who left few words behind
content: Few ancient peoples travelled as far as the Phoenicians, and few left so little of their own testimony. Their harbours occupied a narrow coast, hemmed in by mountains, so the sea became the road available to them. From those harbours they sailed west across the entire span of the middle sea, planting settlements as they advanced. What we know of this civilization comes mostly from others. The Greeks described them as rivals, the Hebrew scriptures as neighbours, and later Roman authors as enemies of a city they had burned. Their own archives were kept on papyrus, which does not survive on a damp coast, therefore the archaeology must carry most of the weight. Excavation at their sites reveals what the texts do not. The settlements were modest at first, chosen for a sheltered bay or an island just offshore, and they served as places to rest, repair, and exchange rather than as farms. Only in later centuries did some expand into cities with walls and their own hinterland. That pattern marks a chain of stations rather than an empire, and it explains why no single capital governed the others. Their most enduring gift travelled with the cargo. The script they used employed a small set of signs for sounds rather than a large set for words, and merchants taught it wherever they stopped. Greeks adopted it, added marks for vowels, and from that line descend most alphabets now used across the west. It is a curious turn in history that a people whose own books are lost should have handed on the means of writing to so many others. Their cities have been excavated, their wrecks located on the sea floor, and their cargoes traced through the clay of the jars, yet the voice of this civilization reaches us only through the mouths of those who wrote about it.

subject: 초원 제국의 구조와 이동
title: How a state on horseback held together
content: The grasslands north of the settled ancient world produced a form of power that farming civilizations found difficult to grasp. There were no walled capitals to capture, no fields to burn, and no season when the enemy could be located in one place. Yet these were genuine states, with courts, ranks, and tribute, and several of them endured for a century or more. Their strength rested on the horse and on the grass. A rider with spare mounts could cover ground at a pace no infantry could match, and the herds that fed the population travelled with them. Because wealth walked on legs, defeat did not destroy the base of power, and a beaten confederation could withdraw far beyond reach and return. This is why the great frontier walls raised against them succeeded only partially. The structure of such an empire differed sharply from that of its neighbours. It was organised in units of tens, hundreds, and thousands, cutting across older ties of kinship, so that a leader could raise a force without seeking permission from every clan. Loyalty ran upward through those units to a single figure at the summit. When that figure died, however, the same structure could split along its seams, and more than one steppe empire disintegrated within a generation of its founder. Commerce mattered as much as warfare. The routes carrying silk, glass, and horses across the middle of the continent passed through this ground, and whoever held it claimed a share. Raiding and trading were not opposites but two methods of drawing the same wealth, and the choice between them followed how willing the settled ancient courts were to open their markets. What the historical record shows, then, is not chaos at the edge of civilization but a different design for holding people together, fitted to grass, distance, and the speed of a horse.

subject: 굽타 시대의 천문 관측
title: Measuring the sky in a classical age
content: The centuries of the Gupta era in northern India are often called classical, and the label suits the sciences quite as well as the arts. Within that span a body of astronomical work was set down in verse, intended to be memorised, and it carried methods that would travel far beyond the subcontinent. One text from the period asserts that the earth rotates on its axis, and that the nightly procession of the constellations results from that rotation rather than from motion in the heavens. Its author supports the claim by comparing the view from a moving boat, where the bank appears to slide past. Such reasoning had surfaced elsewhere in the ancient world, yet here it sits within a working system for computing planetary positions. The mathematics is the striking element. These astronomers employed a place value notation with a symbol for zero, which made lengthy calculation possible on a small surface, and they compiled tables of half chords amounting to a table of sines. With those instruments they predicted eclipses to within a fraction of an hour, and the residual errors were small enough that later generations spent centuries merely trimming them. The knowledge did not remain in place. Manuscripts moved westward through translation, first into Arabic and afterwards into Latin, and the numerals travelled with them. Much of what Europe later called Arabic figures had arrived by this road from India, and the shape of the story recurs throughout history: a method is devised in one civilization, carried by scholars and merchants, and finally credited to whoever transmitted it last. What the record leaves is a reminder that classical need not mean closed. The observers of this era were revising older work, disputing with rivals, and checking their numbers against the sky itself, which is precisely what any living science does.

subject: 참파 왕국의 벽돌 탑
title: Brick towers on a lost coast
content: Along the central coast of what is now Vietnam stand towers of red brick, several of them more than a thousand years old. They were raised by the kingdom of Champa, a civilization that held this shore for many centuries and then faded from the map as its neighbours pressed inward. The towers are much of what survives above ground. Their construction has puzzled visitors since the earliest surveys. The bricks are set so closely that a blade will not pass between them, and no thick layer of mortar appears in the joints. Some early observers supposed the bricks had been rubbed together until they gripped, while others argued for a vegetable resin, and recent analysis points instead to a thin clay slip fired in position. The debate is unsettled, although the result is obvious enough: these walls have survived storms, warfare, and long neglect. Each tower enclosed a shrine, and the carving outside displays figures from the Hindu tradition that reached this coast by sea. Commerce carried more than cargo, since priests, manuscripts, and deities moved along the same routes, and the kings who ruled here adopted titles and rituals from far to the west. Yet the towers do not copy Indian models exactly. Their proportions, the treatment of the brick surface, and the local stone figures mark a style belonging to this place rather than an import. History treated the kingdom harshly. Pressure from the north continued century after century, the ports lost their share of the maritime exchange, and by the late medieval period the state had shrunk to a coastal strip. Its descendants remain, and so does the language, although the courts are gone. Standing among the towers one notices the strange durability of brick and the fragility of everything else, since the walls survive while the archives and ceremonies that filled them do not.

subject: 발해 도성의 배치
title: A northern capital laid out on paper
content: North of the Korean peninsula, on a high plain, lie the traces of a capital raised by the kingdom of Balhae. The state emerged after the fall of an earlier northern power, held a wide territory for more than two centuries, and then collapsed before an army from the steppe. Its written records are thin, therefore the ground plan of the city carries much of what can be learned. The layout follows an ancient model that had spread across the region. A broad avenue runs from the southern gate to the palace at the north, the ground is divided into wards by streets crossing at right angles, and the whole is wrapped within an outer wall. Imperial capitals in China, Japan, and Korea were built on the same principles during this era, so the plan places the kingdom firmly inside a shared world rather than at its margin. Yet the copy is not exact, and the differences matter. The outer wall encloses an enormous area, much of it apparently never built upon, which suggests a plan drawn for a city that never grew into it. The palace platforms rest on a raised terrace, and the heating channels beneath the floors follow a northern design fitted to winters the southern models never faced. Local practice bent the borrowed scheme. What the site says about the state remains disputed. Historians in different countries have claimed the kingdom for their own past, reading the same ancient walls as evidence for one lineage or another. The archaeology alone cannot settle a question that is really about how modern nations narrate their origin. What it can establish is a court that understood the wider order of its time, adopted its forms, and adjusted them to a colder ground and a smaller population than the model had assumed.

subject: 야요이 시대 벼농사의 전파
title: When rice reached the islands
content: The shift from foraging to agriculture in the Japanese islands did not develop slowly from within. It arrived, and the archaeology of the Yayoi era records that arrival in considerable detail. Flooded rice fields, unfamiliar pottery, metal tools, and a new manner of burying the dead appear together within a few centuries, first in the west and afterwards spreading eastward. Before this transition the islands supported one of the longest lasting foraging cultures known anywhere. Its people produced pottery for thousands of years, occupied settled villages, and drew a rich living from nuts, fish, and game without planting grain. That such a stable civilization gave way at all deserves notice, since agriculture is harder labour and its early yields are not obviously superior. Two interpretations have long competed. One holds that people crossed from the mainland in numbers and brought their fields with them. The other holds that the techniques travelled while the population largely remained, learning the new work from a few incomers. Skeletal measurements, and more recently the study of ancient genomes, support a mixed answer: there was genuine movement of people, and there was also blending with those already present. The consequences reached far beyond diet. Rice fields must be flooded and drained on a schedule, which binds a village to a fixed plot and to its neighbours upstream. Stored grain can be counted, taxed, and seized, therefore differences of wealth and rank appear in the graves of this era where earlier burials show almost none. Weapons and defensive ditches appear as well. What the ground records, then, is not merely a new crop but the origin of a new order. Within a few centuries the islands moved from villages of rough equality to small chiefdoms competing for land and water, and the states that later emerged grew from that competition.

subject: 폴리네시아 항해와 섬의 정착
title: Finding islands on purpose
content: The settlement of the Pacific islands ranks among the great achievements in human history. Across a long span of centuries, ancient seafarers moved eastward over an ocean covering a third of the globe, locating specks of land separated by thousands of miles of open water. They accomplished this without written charts and without instruments of the kind later developed in Europe. For a long period outsiders refused to believe it was done deliberately. A popular theory held that canoes had drifted before the wind and struck land by accident, since purposeful voyaging seemed beyond the means available. That theory has been dismantled from several directions. Simulations of currents and winds demonstrate that drift alone would rarely reach the eastern islands, and voyages made in reconstructed canoes have crossed the same waters using traditional methods. Those methods rest on reading many signs simultaneously. Ancient navigators held a mental chart of star paths that rise and set at fixed points on the horizon, and they steered by the sequence of stars through the night. Swell patterns bending around unseen land, the flight of seabirds returning at dusk, cloud formations above an island, and drifting vegetation all narrowed the search. Because such knowledge had to be carried in memory, it was transmitted through chant and long apprenticeship. The archaeology of the era confirms the pattern of the spread. Crops and animals carried deliberately, including taro, breadfruit, pigs, and rats, appear on island after island in a sequence that maps the route. Nobody loads a canoe with livestock while drifting by accident. What the record demonstrates is exploration with a return plan, since a voyager who found nothing had to sail home and report. That combination of daring and method makes this among the most impressive origins any prehistoric civilization can claim.

subject: 절벽 주거지의 건축과 폐기
title: Houses in the cliff, and why they emptied
content: In the canyons of the arid southwest of North America, entire villages sit within hollows in the cliff walls. Rooms of stone and mortar rise several storeys, ladders connect the levels, and circular chambers sunk into the floor served for gathering and ceremony. The builders raised them late in their history, occupied them for only a few generations, and then departed. The setting appears defensive, and frequently it was. The alcoves are difficult to approach, the paths are narrow, and some sites carry walls where the rock alone would not stop a climber. Yet defence explains only part of the choice, since the overhang also shelters walls from rain and captures the low winter sun while shading the summer one. Ancient builders here read their ground closely. The abandonment has generated more argument than the construction. Tree rings from the timbers supply an exceptionally fine record of rainfall, and they reveal a prolonged drought late in the thirteenth century that would have ruined the maize harvest repeatedly. Drought alone, however, cannot be the whole explanation, because the region had endured dry spells before without emptying. Other evidence points to strain within the society itself. Fields had been cultivated hard for generations, timber near the sites was thinning, and indications of violence increase across the final decades. Where people go when land, wood, and trust all fail together is no mystery: the descendants of these villages live in the pueblos to the south, and their oral traditions describe migration rather than disappearance. This matters for how the sites are presented. Older accounts spoke of a vanished civilization, which suited a taste for ruins without heirs. The archaeology and the living communities agree instead on a plainer history, in which a people moved, carried their practices with them, and remain here today.

subject: 올메카 거석 두상의 운반
title: Moving stone heads across a swamp
content: On the humid gulf coast of Mexico stand carved heads of basalt, several taller than a person and weighing many tons. They were produced by the Olmec, the earliest civilization of the region, more than three thousand years ago. Each displays a face beneath a close fitting helmet, and no two are alike, so most scholars read them as portraits of rulers rather than as deities. The ancient carving is remarkable, yet the transport poses the harder puzzle. The stone came from volcanic hills scores of miles from the centres where the heads were erected. Between quarry and city lie swamp, forest, and rivers, and the people who moved these blocks possessed neither draft animals nor wheels in practical use. Therefore every ton had to be shifted by human effort and by water. The favoured explanation combines rollers, sledges, and rafts. Crews could drag a block on log rollers over prepared ground, then float it along the rivers threading the coastal plain, using the current where it assisted and poles where it did not. Experiments with smaller loads suggest the method works, although the labour required is considerable. Estimates run to hundreds of workers for many weeks on a single head. That figure is the genuine historical point. A civilization able to feed such a crew, direct it, and spare it from farming for a season is not a village. The heads are evidence of authority as surely as any wall or throne, and they appear in this era alongside earthen platforms and long distance exchange in jade and obsidian. What the stones record, then, concerns organisation rather than art. Somebody could ask hundreds of people to move a fragment of mountain across a swamp for the sake of one face, and they went. The origin of complex rule in the region is written in that fact.

subject: 마야 도시의 붕괴 연대
title: Reading the dates on a falling civilization
content: The lowland Maya left a gift to those who study them: they carved dates. Monuments record the accession of rulers, their victories, and their ceremonies in a count of days that can be matched to our own calendar with confidence. Because of this, the decline of the southern cities can be traced century by century, and even year by year in places, which is rare for any ancient collapse. What the dates reveal is not a single fall. Carving ceases at different moments in different cities across roughly a hundred and fifty years, beginning in the west and moving eastward. Some centres fall silent while their neighbours are still raising monuments, and a few in the north continue long after the southern heartland has stopped. Therefore the word collapse, if used at all, must cover a rolling process rather than an event. The causes have been argued over for a long period. Cores from lake beds reveal severe drought in the same era, and the region depended on stored rainwater with little reliable surface flow. Warfare also intensified, since the later inscriptions speak more of capture and destruction than the earlier ones do. Soil studies point to erosion after prolonged clearance, and population estimates approach the limit of what the land could carry. No single cause fits every city. What ended was the political order rather than the people. Millions of speakers of Maya languages live in the region today, and the northern cities flourished for centuries after the southern ones went quiet. The archaeology suggests that people left the great centres for smaller settlements, abandoning kings and monuments while keeping farms and households. Read this way, the record is less a mystery than a lesson about which parts of a civilization are fragile. The carved stones stopped because the institution paying for them stopped, not because a population vanished.

subject: 지상화의 제작 방법과 목적
title: Lines on the desert floor
content: On a dry plateau in southern Peru, enormous figures are drawn upon the ground: birds, a monkey, a spider, and straight lines running for miles. They were produced by the Nasca and by ancient people before them, and they have survived for roughly twenty centuries because rain almost never falls there and the wind is steady. How they were produced is the easier question. The surface is covered with dark stones over pale soil, so clearing a strip leaves a light line. Wooden stakes have been recovered at the ends of some lines, and rope stretched between stakes would hold a course straight over long distances. Small sketches nearby suggest the figures were laid out at reduced scale and then enlarged by measured steps, a technique any ancient surveyor would recognise. Why they were produced has resisted a settled answer. An early proposal read the lines as a vast calendar aligned to the rising of stars, but tests against the sky found no better agreement than chance would supply. A more durable idea follows the water. This is among the driest inhabited places on earth, and many lines point toward the localities where streams descend from the highlands or where underground channels reach the surface. Ceremonies petitioning for water would suit a landscape where nothing else mattered as much. The figures may serve a different purpose than the lines. Many appear to be drawn as a single unbroken path, wide enough to walk, which suggests they were made to be travelled along rather than viewed. Since the plateau is flat, no viewpoint on the ground displays a whole figure at once, and their full shape emerges only from the air. That circumstance has fed a great deal of nonsense, although the plainer reading is that the ancient makers walked them and never needed to see them whole.

subject: 누비아 왕국과 이집트의 관계
title: The kingdom upriver that once ruled Egypt
content: South of ancient Egypt, along the same river, lay Nubia, and the two were bound together for thousands of years. Egyptian texts describe the region as a source of gold, ivory, ebony, and soldiers, and for long stretches Egyptian forts held the river crossings. That version of the relation, written by the northern side, dominated how history told the story for a very long period. The archaeology supplies a fuller account. Kingdoms rose upriver with their own cities, temples, and cemeteries, and they dealt as partners rather than serving merely as a supply. Whenever Egypt weakened, the southern states expanded, and one of them eventually did what no Egyptian record could soften: its kings marched north and ruled the entire valley for the better part of a century. Those rulers presented themselves as restorers of ancient tradition. They built in the older style, revived ceremonies that had lapsed, and assumed the full titles of the northern crown. Their pyramids, raised at home upriver, are steeper and smaller than the famous ones downstream, and there are far more of them, since the practice continued in the south for centuries after Egypt had abandoned it. Later kingdoms in the region moved their capital further upstream, developed their own script, and worshipped deities with no northern counterpart. Their queens ruled in their own right often enough that Roman authors remarked upon it. This was a civilization with its own line of development rather than a border province of another. The reason the story is less familiar has to do with how the discipline grew. Early excavation followed the monuments that European visitors already admired, and museums filled with material from the north. Only in the last century, much of it in rescue work before a dam flooded the valley, did the southern record receive comparable attention.

subject: 짐바브웨 석벽의 축조
title: Stone walls that a colony refused to credit
content: In the highlands of southern Africa stands a complex of stone walls, some of them ten metres high, built without mortar of any kind. These blocks are shaped granite, laid in even courses, and the largest enclosure curves in a long unbroken sweep with a conical tower inside its wall. This site was the centre of a state that flourished during the medieval centuries, and its rulers supplied gold and ivory to the coast. Its history within modern scholarship is a case study in how findings can be bent. When European settlers reached the ruins, they insisted the walls could not be African work, and proposed builders from the ancient Mediterranean or the Near East. Early excavations were conducted to prove that thesis, and material contradicting it was discarded. However, careful excavation settled this question early in the twentieth century. The pottery, the layout, and the ordinary household remains are local and continuous with the surrounding culture, and dates from the timbers place the construction in the medieval period rather than in antiquity. Every trained archaeologist who examined the evidence reached the same conclusion, and yet the colonial government of the day pressured museums and guides to present the discredited version to visitors. These walls themselves indicate what their builders were like. Because there is no mortar, stability comes from the taper of each face and from the care of its coursing, which demands long practice. The enclosures separate spaces rather than defend them, since the walls carry no fighting platforms and the openings are wide. This suggests rank and ceremony rather than siege. Imported objects recovered on this site, including beads from India and porcelain from China, reveal a court connected to the ocean world by its rivers and its coast. The origin of that connection was gold, and the decline of the centre follows the shift of the gold routes elsewhere.

subject: 베냉 청동판의 서사
title: A court history cast in metal
content: The medieval palace of the kingdom of Benin, in what is now southern Nigeria, once held hundreds of cast plaques mounted upon its wooden pillars. Each displays figures in relief: the king with attendants, warriors with shields, foreign visitors in hats and beards, and officials whose rank is marked by the number of coral strands at the neck. Together they formed a record that could be read by anyone who knew the code. The casting was done by the lost wax technique, in which a model is shaped in wax over a clay core, covered in further clay, and then heated so the wax escapes and metal replaces it. The results are thin, precise, and detailed enough to display pattern on cloth. Medieval guilds attached to the court held this craft, transmitted it within families, and worked under royal control, therefore the objects are court products rather than independent art. As history the plaques are partial in a useful manner. They show whatever the palace wished remembered, so the king is invariably larger than those around him and the enemy is invariably subdued. Yet the details admitted around the edges preserve information the makers never intended to record, including the dress of foreign visitors, the form of weapons, and the presence of goods from the maritime exchange. Their subsequent fate belongs to the record as well. A British force took the city near the end of the nineteenth century, burned much of it, and carried the plaques away, after which they were dispersed among museums in Europe and America. For a long period they were displayed as work from a nameless civilization rather than as the archive of a specific court. Recent decades have brought both better labelling and a prolonged argument about return, and that argument is itself now part of the history of these objects.

subject: 켈트 철기 시대의 언덕 요새
title: Hills that were shaped into towns
content: Across much of western Europe, hills carry rings of bank and ditch cut during the ancient iron age. Some enclose a small space suitable for a few families, while the largest hold room for hundreds of houses, granaries, and livestock. They were built and rebuilt across several centuries, and they remain among the most visible traces of that era in the landscape. The word fort suits some of them and not others. A few display every mark of warfare: multiple ramparts, staggered entrances that force an attacker to turn, and layers of burning and slingstones in the ground. Others have gaps in the circuit, ditches too shallow to stop anyone, and no indication of violence whatever, so their banks may have marked status or the bounds of a gathering place rather than a defence. Excavation inside the larger sites has altered how they are understood. Rows of round houses, four post structures that probably held raised granaries, and areas of metalworking suggest a settled community rather than a refuge used only in emergency. Some sites appear to have been occupied throughout the year for generations, while others show heavy use at intervals, which suits a seasonal fair or assembly. The pattern differs from region to region. What they reveal about their ancient society is contested. Older accounts read them as the seats of chiefs in a warlike culture, drawing upon Roman descriptions of the ancient tribes. Those descriptions were written by an enemy with reasons to exaggerate, and the archaeology reveals a more varied picture, including long peaceful stretches and wide exchange in salt, iron, and wine. The hills remained in use into the period of Roman contact, and several were taken by force during the conquest. Afterwards most were abandoned, since the new order placed its towns in valleys near roads.

subject: 바이킹 정착지의 발굴
title: Digging up the traders behind the raiders
content: The Norse of the early medieval centuries reached the popular imagination as raiders, and raids they certainly conducted. Yet the archaeological settlements excavated across their historical range tell a broader story, and the ordinary material recovered in them has done more to revise the picture than any written source. Sites in the British Isles, in Ireland, along the rivers of eastern Europe, and in the north Atlantic reveal workshops, warehouses, and dense rows of houses. Finds include scales and folding weights for measuring silver, moulds for casting ornaments, waste from working antler and leather, and coins from a very wide area, including the Islamic world. A raider does not carry precision scales; a merchant does. The waterlogged ground at several of these sites has preserved what usually decays. Timber walls survive to head height in places, along with shoes, combs, textiles, and even the remains of meals, so daily life can be reconstructed in unusual detail. Such preservation explains why these excavations transformed the field, since the written accounts came almost entirely from those who were raided and dwelt on violence for good reason. The north Atlantic sites carry a different lesson. Farms in Iceland and Greenland reveal the strain of settling a landscape that could not bear the agriculture brought from home. Soil erosion followed clearance, the woodland disappeared early, and in Greenland the settlements failed after several centuries under worsening cold. A site on the coast of Newfoundland proves the crossing to the Americas occurred, although the stay was brief. Taken together the excavations describe a mobile medieval civilization doing several things at once. The same ship might trade one season and raid the next, depending on what a coast offered, and the settlements grew where the two activities met. That flexibility, rather than ferocity alone, explains how far these people travelled.

subject: 비잔티움 삼중 성벽의 구조
title: The wall that held a city for a thousand years
content: The land approach to Constantinople was closed by a line of defences built in the early fifth century, and for roughly a thousand years no besieging army broke through it. The design deserves study because it solves the problem of a wide flat approach with layers rather than with a single great barrier. Working outward, an attacker met first a broad ditch that could be flooded, then a low outer wall with its own walkway, then a level terrace, then the main wall rising much higher with towers spaced along its length. Each layer had to be taken in turn, and each was covered by shooting from the one behind and above it. Therefore the defenders could pour fire onto crowded ground while remaining protected, and a breach in the outer line delivered the attacker into a killing terrace rather than into the city. The towers were spaced so that no stretch of wall lay beyond bowshot from at least two of them, and those on the inner and outer lines were staggered rather than aligned, which widened the field of fire. Construction alternated courses of stone and brick, supplying both strength and some flexibility against the earthquakes that struck the region repeatedly through the medieval centuries. Maintenance mattered as much as design. City guilds and districts were assigned stretches to keep in repair, and after major earthquakes the walls were rebuilt within months, since everyone understood what stood between them and the field armies of several empires. The line failed at last against heavy cannon, which could batter masonry faster than crews could shore it. Even then the city held for weeks. What the ruins record is not merely engineering but a civilization organised around a single defensive fact, and the shape of that history is visible in the stone still standing across the modern city.

subject: 사마르칸트 천문대의 관측
title: A prince who measured the stars
content: In the fifteenth century a ruler in Samarkand built an observatory on a hill above the city and spent much of his life using it. He was a grandson of a famous medieval conqueror, and by the standards of his line an unusual figure, since he cared more for the sky than for campaigns. The instrument at the centre of the building was a sextant of enormous size, its arc sunk in a trench cut into the rock so that the whole structure would not shift. Scale was the point. Before optical aids, the accuracy of an angle depended upon how large the marked arc could be made, therefore the way to measure the sky more finely was to build bigger. The arc of this instrument had a radius of about forty metres, so a small fraction of a degree occupied a comfortable span on the scale, and readings could be taken to a precision no earlier observatory of that era had reached. The results appeared in a set of tables giving the positions of more than a thousand stars, along with values for the length of the year and the tilt of the earth's axis. Those numbers were good enough that European astronomers two centuries later found little to correct in them. Because the work was checked by many hands over years rather than taken in a single season, the errors of any one night averaged out. The end of the project was abrupt. The prince was killed shortly after taking the throne, the school around him dispersed, and the building fell into ruin and was quarried for stone. Its position was forgotten until an archaeological excavation early in the twentieth century found the trench with its marked arc still in place. The tables, meanwhile, had travelled by manuscript and outlived the walls that produced them.

subject: 무굴 정원의 배치 원리
title: Gardens laid out as an argument
content: The gardens built by the Mughal court in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries follow a plan that repeats across a wide range of sites. A walled rectangle is divided into four by water channels crossing at the centre, and each quarter is divided again, so the whole reads as a grid. Paths run beside the channels, trees are set in rows, and a pavilion or a tomb stands where the axes meet. The plan arrived with the ruling dynasty of that era from central Asia and drew upon ancient Persian practice. Its shape carried meaning, since the four rivers and the enclosed paradise of scripture were understood by everyone who walked in it. Yet the design also solved practical problems in a hot climate, because moving water cools the air, shade trees line the walks, and the walls exclude dust and wind. Water is the demanding element. Channels must run at a slight steady fall, and keeping them full through a dry season meant tanks, wells, and sometimes aqueducts from a distant source. In the gardens built among the hills of Kashmir the slope was used instead, with terraces stepping down and small cascades between them, and the sound of falling water became part of the design. Tombs followed the same plan. The most famous of them stands at the northern edge of its garden rather than at the centre, which breaks the older pattern and sets the building against the river beyond. Historians of the empire still argue about whether this was a change in meaning or a response to the site. Later centuries treated these grounds as ornament and allowed many of them to decay, while colonial restoration frequently replaced flowerbeds and cypress rows with lawns in the English taste. Recent work has tried to recover the original planting from court accounts.

subject: 원대 역참망의 운영
title: The relay network that held an empire together
content: The Mongol empire of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries covered more ground than any state had before, and holding it required moving orders and reports across distances that took months on foot. The answer was a network of relay stations, spaced roughly a day's ride apart along the main routes, each stocked with horses, fodder, and lodging. A rider carrying an official tablet could take a fresh mount at every station and pass his message onward, so news travelled at a pace that astonished visitors. Accounts from the era speak of several hundred miles in a day for urgent dispatches, using riders who changed constantly while the message did not stop. Therefore the court could learn of trouble on a distant frontier within weeks rather than seasons. The cost fell upon the settlements near each station. They supplied the animals and the grain, and complaints about the burden appear steadily in the records of these centuries, since a passing official with a tablet could requisition whatever he liked. Attempts to limit abuse by restricting who received tablets recur across the whole period, which suggests the problem was never solved. The network carried more than orders. Merchants travelled its roads under protection, and so did craftsmen, priests, and envoys from far outside the empire. The famous accounts written by European and Muslim travellers of this era were possible because the system existed, and the exchange of goods and knowledge across the continent owes a great deal to it. When the empire broke apart, the stations decayed unevenly. Successor states kept the sections that served them and allowed the remainder to lapse, and the long through routes that had crossed the whole continent were cut into segments. What had made the era exceptional was not the roads themselves but the single authority that kept every station on them supplied.

subject: 에도의 상수도 체계
title: Bringing clean water to a huge early city
content: By the eighteenth century the city now called Tokyo held more than a million residents, which made it one of the largest cities in history to that date. Its site posed a problem, since much of the low ground had been reclaimed from marsh and the wells there yielded brackish water. A city of that size could not run on bad wells, therefore water had to be brought in from elsewhere. This answer took the form of a network of channels drawing from rivers and from a lake to the west. These channels ran by gravity into the city, and their water then entered wooden conduits laid beneath the streets. Shafts lined with stone or timber allowed households to draw from these buried pipes with buckets, so what resembled a well was frequently a tap on a distant river. Two main lines served the greater part of the city, and their construction dates to the early decades of the era. Although the design itself was simple, its maintenance was organised in detail. Officials inspected these channels, cleared their silt, and replaced the wooden pipes, which rot and therefore had to be renewed on a cycle. Rules forbade washing or dumping upstream, and neighbourhood associations bore responsibility for the sections serving them. Because the system ran on gravity alone, a blockage anywhere upstream affected everyone below, which gave every district a stake in the whole. This design had a further consequence for the shape of the city. Fire was the constant danger in a place built of wood and paper, and the same channels supplied the crews and the barrels kept along the streets. Historians of the era note that the water network and the fire brigades developed together. When modern pipes arrived in the late nineteenth century, the old wooden conduits were dug up in stretches, and sections survive in museums as evidence of an early urban system of that civilization.

subject: 흑사병 이후의 인구 회복
title: How long a continent took to fill again
content: The plague that swept Europe in the middle of the fourteenth century killed somewhere between a third and a half of the people within a few years. What followed is in some respects more interesting than the mortality itself, since the recovery took far longer than a simple count of births would predict, and the delay reshaped the whole medieval order. Numbers did not rebound because the plague did not depart. It returned in waves every decade or two for the next three centuries, striking children hardest in the later outbreaks, so each generation lost part of its replacement. Estimates suggest the continent did not regain its earlier level until the sixteenth century, and in some regions later than that. Therefore the century after the first outbreak was one of persistent scarcity of people. The consequences ran through everything. Land was suddenly abundant relative to labour, so wages rose and rents fell, and the ties binding peasants to particular estates weakened wherever lords could not enforce them. Attempts to legislate wages back down appear across the region within a few years of the first outbreak, which is good evidence that conditions were moving against landholders. Revolts follow in several countries within a generation. Settlement patterns changed as well. Marginal fields cleared during the crowded decades before the plague were abandoned, and the archaeology of deserted villages across this era records the retreat. Land returned to pasture, and wool and meat took a larger share of production than grain. What the period demonstrates is how a shock to a population works its way through a whole civilization over generations rather than years. The plague ended quickly in any given town; its effect on wages, tenure, and the use of land was still visible when the continent finally filled again more than a century and a half later.
